headline: High: Chatwoot’s broad network egress plus shared content workflows create leakage and cascading-action risk; prompt-injection risk is limited by the non-runnable prompt-engineering repo.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a non-runnable prompt-engineering repository with no I/O surfaces, so it cannot directly ingest B’s outputs. B has integrations and broad egress, but there is no documented shared channel or parser bridge between them. The only plausible pathway is manual copy/paste or external reuse of content, which is low blast radius.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies B-generated text into A-derived prompts or templates, prompt injection becomes possible.
IF a shared filesystem or MCP bridge is added later, the pathway changes from manual to automated.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Avoid copying raw B outputs into prompt templates.
Add a short human review step before reusing generated text.
Disable any future shared clipboard or MCP bridge unless provenance is tracked.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tagging if automated transfer is introduced.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, messages, and reports, and it has broad network egress. A is a content-writing repo with no runtime surfaces, so it is not itself a leak source, but if A is used to draft or transform B content, sensitive data can be exposed through B’s outbound integrations or external services. The pairwise risk exists in default B workflows.
conditions: IF B forwards customer messages or reports to any connected API, those data classes can leave the system.
IF A is used to rewrite or summarize B content before export, sensitive fields may be preserved in the output.
mitigations: Restrict B integrations to approved destinations.
Redact customer identifiers before any outbound send.
Review one sample outbound payload from each integration.
Keep A away from raw customer exports.
requires-engineering: add DLP or field-level masking on B egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no declared write or network capabilities and is not runnable, while B only shows broad network egress and API integrations. There is no documented shared mutable resource, filesystem, or overlapping write scope, so direct capability conflict is not evidenced. Any conflict would require an added shared workspace or external orchestrator not present in the profiles.
conditions: IF both agents are later granted write access to the same directory or ticketing system, write conflicts become plausible.
IF an orchestrator adds shared locks or queues, the current low risk may change.
mitigations: Do not grant shared write access by default.
Separate B’s integration credentials from any A-related workflow.
Use distinct folders for drafts and customer records.
Check for accidental overlap in API tokens.
requires-engineering: add locking if both agents must mutate the same resource.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B can act on customer-support workflows and integrations, so if it consumes A-generated text as authoritative, errors can cascade into customer-facing actions. A is a prompt-engineering content source, not a verified fact engine, which increases the chance that B treats unverified guidance as operational input. The pathway is plausible in default content-reuse workflows, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF B uses A-produced text as a source for replies, macros, or integration payloads without verification, errors can propagate.
IF B auto-sends responses or updates tickets based on that text, downstream impact increases.
mitigations: Require human review before sending A-derived content through B.
Mark A outputs as non-authoritative in workflow docs.
Use templates that separate facts from generated prose.
Spot-check one customer reply path end-to-end.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before B executes actions from generated text.

E_compliance.rationale: B processes customer data and related records, while A is an open-source content repository with no declared data handling. The pair itself does not prove a residency or certification mismatch, but B’s outbound integrations and customer-data scope create a compliance exposure if regulated data is routed through external services or reused in A-derived content. Uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is sent from B to any external integration without a DPA or residency review, compliance risk materializes.
IF A-derived content includes customer identifiers and is stored in public or uncontrolled repos, retention and disclosure issues arise.
mitigations: Confirm which B integrations receive customer data.
Avoid placing customer data into A-linked public artifacts.
Document retention for outbound support transcripts.
Review whether any integration crosses residency boundaries.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
